name: Minnis Bay sunset and the Reculver Towers silhouette
summary: Birchington's own west-facing sunset spot: wide sands, groynes and, around the equinoxes, the sun dropping behind distant Reculver Towers.
description: Minnis Bay is the westernmost beach of Birchington and the point where Thanet's chalk gives way to the flat former Wantsum Channel. Because the coast turns west here, the bay is one of the few places in Thanet with an open sea-and-marsh horizon towards the setting sun. The twin towers of Reculver stand almost exactly due west, about 6 km away, so around the spring and autumn equinoxes (late March and late September) the sun sets close to them: a long lens of 300 mm or more turns the towers into a crisp silhouette against the disc. In midsummer the sun sets further round to the north-west, out over the sea, giving long glowing twilights over wet sand at low tide. The timber groynes, the sailing club's dinghies and the sea wall promenade make good foreground lines, and wet sand at low water gives mirror reflections. The bay holds a Blue Flag and has a car park, café and toilets by the promenade.
price: Free; car park by the bay is pay-and-display (fee per OSM).
dogs: Seasonal dog restrictions apply on Thanet beaches; check Thanet District Council signage.
accessibility: Level concrete promenade along the sea wall; slipways down to the sand.
tips: Use a sun-position app: the sun sits on the Reculver Towers line (azimuth about 269 degrees) only for a few days either side of each equinox. Bring a long lens and arrive 45 minutes early.
best_time: Sunset all year; equinoxes for the sun behind Reculver Towers due west; midsummer for sunsets over the sea to the NW; winter sunsets are further south over the marshes.
tide: Low or falling tide exposes wide wet sand for reflections; at high water the sea reaches the sea wall and groynes become the subject.
wildlife: Turnstones feed and roost along this coast in winter (roughly October to March); keep back from roosting flocks at high tide.
facilities: Pay car park, café, toilets and Minnis Bay Sailing Club by the promenade.

name: Minnis Bay groynes and reef: winter waders
summary: Low-angle wader photography on the groynes and chalk reef of Minnis Bay, where turnstones gather each winter.
description: The chalk foreshore and wooden groynes around Minnis Bay and the neighbouring small bays east towards Grenham Bay are a winter feeding ground for waders. Turnstones are the stars: they arrive from breeding grounds in Arctic Canada and the tundra and return to the same Thanet bays each winter, flipping seaweed and stones for crabs and shrimps. The Thanet Coast Project describes the numbers along North East Kent as internationally important, and the stretch from Reculver to Birchington has signed high-tide roosts. For photographers the trick is to lie low on the sand or sit still on the groyne ends as the tide drops, letting the birds work towards you, and to shoot at eye level with a 400-600 mm lens. Birders also look for sanderling along the tideline and for purple sandpiper on the groynes and reef edge, though these are less regular. Please never flush a roost: disturbed birds burn energy they cannot spare in winter.
dogs: Keep dogs on a lead near feeding or roosting birds (Thanet Coast Project advice).
accessibility: Promenade is level; the reef and groynes are slippery, uneven and weed-covered.
tips: Go 1-2 hours either side of high water, when birds are pushed close to the sea wall, but stay well back from the actual roost. Overcast days give soft, even light on grey plumage.
best_time: October to March; morning light from the east lights the birds when you shoot westwards along the groynes.
tide: Rising tide pushes waders towards the shore; falling tide opens the reef for feeding. The chalk reef is slippery: watch the incoming tide around the groyne ends.
wildlife: Turnstone October-March (internationally important numbers on the North East Kent coast). Sanderling and purple sandpiper are reported by local birders in winter (not confirmed from an official source).
facilities: Car park, toilets and café at Minnis Bay.

name: Grenham Bay and Epple Bay chalk coves
summary: Small chalk-cliffed coves east of Minnis Bay, with stacks, reef and beach huts for close-in coastal compositions.
description: East of Minnis Bay the coast rises into low white cliffs cut into a chain of small sandy coves: Grenham Bay, Beresford Gap and Epple Bay, all reachable along the lower promenade. They are much more intimate than Minnis Bay's wide sands, with chalk walls, small stacks, flint bands and a wave-cut chalk platform that is exposed at low water. The coves face north, so in summer the evening sun rakes across the cliff faces from the north-west, and at dawn in midsummer the low sun lights them from the north-east. The chalk platform is full of pools and weed, so this is also good ground for macro work on shore life at low tide. Local turnstone roosts are signed along this coast, so keep clear of resting flocks at high tide.
address: Grenham Bay / Epple Bay, Birchington, Kent
dogs: Seasonal beach dog rules apply; check council signage.
accessibility: Lower promenade is level; access down to each cove is by slopes or steps.
tips: Midsummer evenings give warm side-light on the cliffs; overcast days suit long exposures of water around the chalk.
best_time: Summer evenings for side-light on the cliffs; any calm low tide for reef and pools.
tide: Low tide exposes the chalk platform and pools. Do not round the headlands between coves on a rising tide; stay off the base of the cliffs, which shed chalk.
wildlife: Turnstone in winter; shore crabs, anemones and seaweeds in the pools.

name: Reculver Towers at sunset
summary: Twin 12th-century church towers on the edge of the sea, the most recognisable silhouette on the North Kent coast.
description: The two towers at Reculver are the ruins of St Mary's church, founded in 669 inside the Roman fort of Regulbium and given its twin towers in the late 12th century. When the church was demolished in 1809, Trinity House bought what was left in 1810 to keep the towers as a sea mark, and they still serve mariners as a landmark today. In the Second World War the coast here was used to test prototypes of Barnes Wallis's bouncing bomb, with the towers as the aiming landmark. For photographers the towers work from almost every side: from the sea wall to the east they stand against the evening sky, from the beach at low tide they reflect in wet sand, and from the country park cliffs to the west they line up with sunrise over Thanet. The sea wall and groynes make strong leading lines. A visitor centre, café and pub sit beside the car park.
address: Reculver Lane, Reculver, Herne Bay, Kent
opening_hours: Exterior of towers and fort site open access at any reasonable time.
price: Free; car park beside the towers is pay (fee per OSM).
accessibility: Level sea wall path from the car park; grass around the towers.
tips: Shoot from the sea wall east of the towers (towards Minnis Bay) for sunset behind them; in summer the sun sets to the NW over the sea, in winter to the SW over the land.
best_time: Sunset from the east side, sunrise from the west (country park cliffs); stormy winter skies are dramatic.
tide: Low tide gives wet-sand reflections and groyne lines; at high water waves hit the sea wall (stay back in rough seas).
wildlife: Turnstone roosts signed along the Reculver-Birchington shore in winter.
facilities: Pay car park, Reculver Visitor Centre, toilets and café/pub next to the towers.

name: Reculver Towers: astrophotography and night skies
summary: One of the darker coastal spots near Thanet, with the towers as a ready-made foreground for stars and the Milky Way.
description: Reculver sits between the towns of Herne Bay and Thanet, with the open water of the Thames Estuary to the north and the flat, largely unlit Wantsum marshes to the east. That makes it one of the better places close to Birchington for night photography, although it is not a designated dark-sky site: the glow of Herne Bay to the west and Thanet's towns to the east is visible on the horizon. The towers give a strong, recognisable foreground, and on calm nights they can be light-painted gently or lit by the low ambient glow. Looking north over the sea, summer nights from June to early July are the season to watch for noctilucent clouds after sunset, and the northern horizon is dark water. The summer Milky Way rises in the south-east to south, over land, so frame it from the beach side looking inland towards the towers. The car park is beside the towers, so kit does not have to be carried far.
opening_hours: Open access; check car park terms for overnight stays.
accessibility: Short level walk from the car park.
tips: Pick a moonless night with a north-east wind to push town haze away. A headtorch with red light keeps night vision for other photographers.
best_time: Moonless nights; Milky Way core low in the south May-August; noctilucent clouds to the north June-July; winter for Orion over the towers.
tide: Not critical; keep off the beach below the sea wall at high water in the dark.
facilities: Pay car park beside the towers; no lighting on the sea wall.

name: Wantsum marshes sea wall (Minnis Bay to Reculver)
summary: Flat, unlit grazing marsh on the old Wantsum Channel: big skies for astro, mist at dawn and marsh birds.
description: Between Minnis Bay and Reculver the sea wall runs for several kilometres beside the low marshes of the former Wantsum Channel, which once made Thanet a true island. Inland there are drainage dykes, grazing fields and farmland with almost no buildings or streetlights, so this is the darkest stretch of ground within walking distance of Birchington. Astrophotographers can set up anywhere along the wall with a clear 360-degree horizon; the main light domes are Herne Bay to the west and the Thanet towns to the east. At dawn on still autumn mornings, mist pools over the dykes and the Reculver Towers rise out of it, and in winter the fields hold wildfowl and the open sky suits watching birds of prey hunting. The route is part of the coastal path, but there is no shelter and it is exposed to wind off the estuary.
address: Sea wall path between Minnis Bay and Reculver
opening_hours: Open access on the public coastal path.
dogs: Keep dogs on leads near grazing livestock and birds.
accessibility: Firm, level sea wall path; long distances with no facilities between the ends.
tips: Park at Minnis Bay or Reculver and walk 1-2 km along the wall to escape car park lights. Dew forms fast on the marsh: bring lens heaters.
best_time: Moonless clear nights for astro; calm autumn dawns for mist; winter afternoons for raptors over the marsh.
wildlife: Wildfowl and waders on the fields and foreshore in winter (species not confirmed from an official source).
facilities: Facilities only at Minnis Bay and Reculver.

name: Reculver Country Park and Bishopstone Glen
summary: Soft cliffs, a wooded glen and a clifftop viewpoint looking east to the Reculver Towers.
description: Reculver Country Park covers about 64 acres of clifftop grassland and runs roughly 1.5 miles west from the Roman fort to Bishopstone Glen. It is managed by Canterbury City Council together with Kent Wildlife Trust. The cliffs here are soft sands and clays, not chalk, and they slump and erode, creating raw, layered faces and fans of material on the beach. Bishopstone Glen is a steep gully cut down to the shore, with scrub and trees that hold warblers and insects in summer. From the clifftop viewpoint at the glen the towers stand at the far end of the bay, making a classic elevated composition at sunrise or in the blue hour. In summer the grassland is good for butterflies and other macro subjects. Car parks at Reculver Drive and at the park are free according to OpenStreetMap.
address: Bishopstone Lane / Reculver Drive, Herne Bay, Kent
accessibility: Clifftop paths are grass and gravel; the glen is steep with steps.
tips: Stand at the Bishopstone Glen viewpoint for sunrise behind the towers in winter, when the sun rises in the south-east over Thanet.
best_time: Winter sunrise for the towers from the west; summer days for butterflies on the grassland.
tide: The beach below the cliffs can be cut off by high tide; cliffs are unstable, keep clear of the base.
wildlife: Summer grassland insects and butterflies; scrub birds in the glen (species not confirmed).
facilities: Free car parks at Reculver Drive and Bishopstone (per OSM); visitor centre at Reculver.

name: Westgate cliffs: West Bay and St Mildred's Bay
summary: Two sheltered chalk bays with Victorian promenades, beach huts, a wide chalk reef and good rock pools at low tide.
description: Westgate-on-Sea, the next town east of Birchington, has two neat bays set into low chalk cliffs: West Bay and St Mildred's Bay, joined by a lower promenade. Both look north over the estuary and dry out at low tide to a broad chalk platform. The Thanet Coast Project filmed one of its seashore safaris at West Bay, which makes it a good place for macro work in the pools: crabs, small fish such as the shanny, anemones and seaweeds. The rows of beach huts, the curve of the promenade and the cliffs make clean architectural compositions, especially in the warm side-light of a summer evening. Turnstone high-tide roosts are signed along the Westgate shore in winter. Each bay has a café, and there is a pay car park at St Mildred's Bay.
dogs: Seasonal beach dog restrictions; check signage.
accessibility: Level lower promenade; ramps down to both beaches.
tips: Low spring tides expose the most reef; bring a polariser to cut glare off the pools.
best_time: Summer evenings for side-lit cliffs and huts; low spring tides for pools; winter for turnstones.
tide: Low tide exposes the chalk reef; walk back before the flood tide fills the gullies. Stay away from cliff bases.
wildlife: Turnstone roosts in winter; shore life in the pools year-round.
facilities: Cafés at West Bay and St Mildred's Bay; pay car park at St Mildred's Bay; Westgate station nearby.

name: Margate Harbour Arm and Turner Contemporary (blue hour)
summary: Stone pier, lighthouse, Gormley's sea statue and a gallery whose skies once inspired Turner: Margate's best blue-hour spot.
description: Margate's old stone harbour arm curls out from the Droit House to a small lighthouse, enclosing the harbour beside the Turner Contemporary gallery. The gallery, designed by David Chipperfield and opened in 2011, is a cluster of pale, angular blocks that glow when lit at dusk and photograph well from the end of the arm. On the rocks just off the gallery stands Another Time, one of Antony Gormley's iron figures, which is gradually submerged by the rising tide and is a favourite long-exposure subject. Margate faces north-west across the estuary, so in summer the sun sets over the sea and the light is famous for the reason J.M.W. Turner liked it. Turn round after sunset and the Main Sands, the seafront and Dreamland's lights give a blue-hour cityscape. The harbour arm has bars and small galleries, and the Droit House houses visitor information.
address: Margate Harbour Arm, Stone Pier, Margate, Kent
opening_hours: Harbour arm open access. Turner Contemporary: Tue-Sun and bank holidays 10:00-17:00, closed Monday (per OSM; check gallery site). Droit House 10:00-17:00.
accessibility: Harbour arm is level paving; the gallery is step-free.
tips: Time it so the tide is around half height: Another Time is then partly covered and waves wash around it. A 6-10 stop ND smooths the water.
best_time: Summer sunsets over the sea to the NW; blue hour all year; winter for sunsets earlier in the evening with fewer crowds.
tide: Another Time is covered at high tide and stands clear at low; mid-tide gives the best water movement. Keep off the slippery lower steps.
wildlife: Turnstones use Margate harbour as a high-tide and night roost in winter.
facilities: Bars and cafés on the arm, visitor information at the Droit House, pay car parks on the seafront, Margate station 10 minutes' walk.

name: Walpole Bay Tidal Pool, Cliftonville
summary: A huge 1930s sea-filled pool on the chalk reef: geometric walls, mirror water and pastel sunrises.
description: Below the cliffs at Cliftonville, Walpole Bay holds one of the largest tidal pools in Britain, built in the 1930s by walling off a large area of the chalk foreshore so that seawater is trapped as the tide falls. At low tide the pool's straight concrete walls stand out across the reef, giving bold geometric lines; at high tide it disappears beneath the sea. On calm mornings the pool becomes a mirror for the sky and for the swimmers who use it all year round. Aerial-style views are possible from the clifftop promenade, and the Victorian lift and slope down from the cliffs add context. The surrounding reef was one of the Thanet Coast Project's seashore safari film locations and is good for rock pools and macro. Free to use and open at all times.
opening_hours: Open access (pool usable when the tide is out).
accessibility: Slope down from the clifftop; the pool walls and reef are uneven and slippery.
tips: Use a tide table: arrive as the falling tide first exposes the walls for the cleanest reflections. Respect swimmers' privacy when photographing.
best_time: Calm summer dawns (sun rising to the NE); low tide for the walls; any season for swimmers.
tide: Exposed and usable at low tide; covered at high tide. Do not stay on the outer walls as the tide floods.
wildlife: Seaweeds, crabs and small fish on the chalk reef.
facilities: Street and car park parking on the clifftop; Walpole Bay Hotel above.

name: Foreness Point
summary: Thanet's north-eastern headland: sea-watching for passing seabirds and a landfall for autumn migrants.
description: Foreness Point is the blunt headland between Palm Bay and Botany Bay where the Thanet coast turns from facing north to facing east. Because it juts out into the sea, it is used by local birders as a sea-watching point, scanning for seabirds moving along the coast, and the clifftop scrub and grass can hold tired migrants after easterly winds in spring and autumn. The foreshore below is part of the wide chalk reef, and the Thanet Coast Project has put up signs for turnstone roosts along the Foreness to Botany Bay coast. For landscape photographers the point gives views both west along the cliffs and south-east towards the Botany Bay stacks, and the clifftop is a dawn spot in summer with the sun rising over the sea to the north-east.
dogs: Keep dogs on a lead near roosting birds.
accessibility: Clifftop grass and promenade; reef access by steps or slopes.
tips: For seabirds, come early on a morning with onshore (north to north-east) winds and bring a scope or long lens.
best_time: Spring and autumn migration with easterly winds; summer sunrise to the NE.
tide: Low tide exposes the reef; the bays either side can be cut off by the rising tide.
wildlife: Seabird passage and migrants in spring and autumn (species not confirmed from an official source); turnstone roosts in winter.

name: Botany Bay chalk stacks
summary: Thanet's most photographed beach: white cliffs, chalk stacks and reef, lit by summer sunrises over the sea.
description: Botany Bay is the northernmost of Broadstairs' seven bays, a sandy beach walled by bright chalk cliffs with free-standing chalk stacks on the shore. It is the classic Thanet seascape and is busy with day-trippers in summer. The coast here is actively eroding: the bay's best-known stack collapsed in 2024, a reminder that the stacks and cliffs are always changing and can fall without warning. The remaining stacks, especially at the eastern end, still make striking foregrounds, and at low tide the chalk reef, pools and weed-covered boulders give layers for wide-angle and long-exposure shots. The bay faces north-east, so it is a sunrise spot from late spring to late summer when the sun comes up over the sea, and its pale cliffs glow pink in the first light. Lifeguards patrol in summer. A kiosk sits at the top of the beach access.
price: Free (parking on nearby streets / pay car parks).
dogs: Seasonal dog restrictions apply on Thanet beaches in summer; check signage.
accessibility: Steep slope down to the beach; sand and reef beyond.
tips: Arrive before sunrise in June-July for empty sand. Never stand under or lean on the stacks or cliff face.
best_time: Summer sunrise (sun rises to the NE over the sea); stormy winter days for waves; moonless nights for stars over the stacks to the north.
tide: Low tide exposes the reef and lets you walk between stacks; the rising tide fills the bay quickly and can cut off the route round to Kingsgate Bay. Cliffs and stacks are unstable.
wildlife: Turnstone roosts signed along the Foreness-Botany Bay coast in winter; shore life in the pools.
facilities: Beach kiosk; lifeguards in summer (May-September in 2024); hotel and pub above.

name: Kingsgate Bay and Kingsgate Castle
summary: A small, enclosed chalk bay beneath a castle-style clifftop house, with caves and sea-cut chalk.
description: Just east of Botany Bay, Kingsgate Bay is a narrow, sheltered cove whose chalk walls have been cut by the sea into caves and hollows. Above it stands Kingsgate Castle, a castellated house on the clifftop that makes the bay feel like a scene from a much wilder coast. The bay faces north-east, so early light from the sea lights the chalk and the castle walls on summer mornings. Inside the cove, the curved cliffs, caves and boulders lend themselves to intimate wide-angle compositions and to long exposures of waves running into the gullies. At low tide the reef connects round towards Botany Bay. The bay is smaller and quieter than its neighbour, and the castle itself is private.
opening_hours: Open access to the beach; Kingsgate Castle is private.
accessibility: Steep access down to the beach.
tips: Combine with Botany Bay on the same falling tide, but check your timing before walking round the headland.
best_time: Summer sunrise; low tide for exploring the cove.
tide: Low tide only for walking round the headlands; the cove fills on the rising tide and the return route can be cut off. Keep away from the cliff base and cave roofs.

name: Joss Bay
summary: Thanet's surf beach: an east-facing sandy bay for sunrise, surf action and chalk cliff lines.
description: Joss Bay sits in a dip in the cliffs between Kingsgate and North Foreland and is the main surfing beach of Thanet, with a surf school and a beach café. It faces east out to sea, so it is one of the most reliable spots on the island for sunrise over the water at any time of year, with the sun climbing out of the sea from the north-east in summer and the south-east in winter. The beach is sandy with chalk cliffs either side and a chalk reef at the edges, and when a swell is running, surfers make good action subjects for a telephoto lens. The North Foreland lighthouse is a short walk south along the cliff road. A large pay car park sits right behind the beach.
dogs: Seasonal dog restrictions in summer; check signage.
accessibility: Slope from the car park to the sand.
tips: Winter sunrises are later and further south, so the sun rises over the cliffs at the south end; summer sunrise is straight out to sea.
best_time: Sunrise all year; autumn and winter swells for surf.
tide: Low tide widens the beach and exposes the reef at the sides; the bays round the headlands cut off on the rising tide.
facilities: Pay car park, Joss Bay Café, surf school, toilets (seasonal).

name: North Foreland Lighthouse
summary: The last Trinity House lighthouse to be automated, on Thanet's eastern cliff top; great for night and star-trail shots.
description: A light has shone from North Foreland since 1636, and the present 26 m tower dates mainly from 1792, modernised between 1858 and 1866. It was automated in 1998 in a ceremony with the Duke of Edinburgh, the last manned Trinity House lighthouse to be switched over. The 1860 lens is still in use, and the light shows five white and red flashes every 20 seconds with a range of about 19 nautical miles. The tower stands among houses and keepers' cottages (now holiday lets) and is not open to the public, so photographs are taken from the public roads and verges around it. At night the turning beam makes a good subject for long exposures and star trails over the white tower; by day the tower pairs well with a telephoto from the Joss Bay side.
opening_hours: Exterior view only from public roads; the lighthouse is not open to visitors.
accessibility: Roadside views; pavements on surrounding residential roads.
tips: Respect residents: no tripods blocking drives. Exposures of 20 seconds or a multiple capture one full flash sequence.
best_time: Blue hour and night when the light is working; clear nights for star trails.
facilities: No facilities; Joss Bay car park and café are nearby.

name: Viking Bay, Broadstairs
summary: A horseshoe of sand below Broadstairs' clifftop town, with the little harbour pier and Bleak House on the skyline.
description: Viking Bay is the curving town beach of Broadstairs, framed by chalk cliffs, the old harbour pier with its fishing boats, and the clifftop houses including Bleak House, linked with Charles Dickens. It faces east, so the sunrise comes up over the sea and lights the town, while in the evening the bay falls into shade and the town lights come on, making it a good blue-hour subject from the end of the pier looking back. The pastel beach huts, the lift and the Victorian promenade add colour and pattern for detail shots. South of the bay, the cliff path leads on to Louisa Bay and Stone Bay to the north, each with chalk reef at low tide. In summer the beach is very busy; early mornings are calm.
dogs: Seasonal dog restrictions on the main beach in summer; check signage.
accessibility: Lift and slopes down from the promenade; harbour pier is level.
tips: Shoot from the pier head back towards the town at blue hour; at sunrise shoot from the clifftop gardens out over the pier.
best_time: Sunrise over the sea (east-facing); blue hour for the lit town; winter weekdays for empty sand.
tide: Low tide extends the beach and exposes chalk ledges at the sides.
facilities: Cafés, toilets and pubs around the bay; pay car parks in town; Broadstairs station.

name: Dumpton Gap and Thanet chalk-reef rock pools
summary: Macro on the longest continuous stretch of coastal chalk habitat in England: pools, crabs, fish and weed at low tide.
description: Thanet's shore is lined by a wave-cut chalk platform that the Thanet Coast Project describes as the longest continuous stretch of coastal chalk habitat in the country, protected within the North East Kent Marine Protected Area. At low tide it becomes a maze of pools, gullies and weed beds. The project filmed its seashore safaris at Dumpton Gap (Broadstairs), Walpole Bay (Margate), Eastcliff (Ramsgate), West Bay (Westgate) and Stone Bay (Broadstairs), so all are proven rock-pooling spots. Dumpton Gap, a small cove between Broadstairs and Ramsgate, is a good base. Expect shannies, velvet swimming crabs and shore crabs, anemones, sponges and red and green seaweeds; on the strandline, egg cases of skates, rays and sharks are found. For macro, a polariser cuts surface glare, and a clear-bottomed viewing box or a quick dip with a waterproof camera gets you under the reflections. Return any stones you turn exactly as you found them.
opening_hours: Open access; low tide only for the reef.
accessibility: Slope down to the beach; reef is very slippery.
tips: Aim for low spring tides (around new and full moon). Follow the Thanet Coastal Codes and the project's 'Rockpooling Responsibly' advice. Seashore Safari events run with guides.
best_time: Low spring tides, spring to autumn; calm days for clear water.
tide: Go out on a falling tide and head back as it turns; gullies fill fast and can cut you off from the beach. Wear grippy footwear.
wildlife: Year-round shore life: shanny, velvet swimming crab, shore crab, anemones, seaweeds; mermaid's purses on the strandline.
facilities: Small car parks near Dumpton Gap (OSM); facilities in Broadstairs.

name: Ramsgate Royal Harbour at night
summary: The UK's only Royal Harbour: a marina of masts, a red-lit lighthouse and Regency waterfront that come alive after dark.
description: Ramsgate is the only harbour in the UK allowed to call itself a Royal Harbour, a title granted by George IV in 1821. Its marina has about 700 berths, mostly in the inner basin behind lock gates, so on still nights the water mirrors masts, the floodlit Regency and Victorian buildings of the waterfront, and the arches under Royal Parade. On the end of the West Pier stands an 11 m Grade II listed lighthouse of 1842, designed by John Shaw Jr., which shows a fixed red light and carries the motto 'Perfugium miseris' (refuge for the wretched). The obelisk on the quay and the clock house add more subjects. Walk out along the West Pier for a view back across the harbour to the town, or shoot down from the cliff-top promenade for a wide view of the basin at blue hour.
opening_hours: Harbour piers and promenade open access (pier access may close in storms).
accessibility: Level quays and piers; cliff-top promenade reached by ramps and steps.
tips: Calm, cold winter nights give the stillest water; shoot during blue hour for a balance of sky and lights.
best_time: Blue hour and night all year; sunrise from the East Pier (harbour faces south-east).
tide: The inner marina is held behind lock gates, so reflections work at any tide; the outer harbour drains at low tide.
wildlife: Turnstones often roost and feed on harbour walls in winter; seal trips leave from here.
facilities: Cafés, pubs, toilets and pay car parks around the harbour; Ramsgate station 15 minutes' walk.

name: Hugin Viking ship replica, Pegwell Bay
summary: A full-size replica longship on the clifftop above Pegwell Bay, sailed over from Denmark in 1949.
description: On the grass above Pegwell Bay beside the main road stands Hugin, a full-size replica of a Viking longboat. It was sailed from Denmark in 1949 to mark the traditional landing of the Anglo-Saxons in this part of Kent, and it was restored in 2004-05. With its dragon prow, curved hull and striped shield line, it is an unusual and characterful subject, especially when lit by low evening sun or shot at blue hour against the sky. From the clifftop behind it there are views across the mudflats and saltmarsh of Pegwell Bay towards Sandwich Bay, with the former hoverport pad below (the only remains of the 1969-1992 hovercraft terminal).
address: Pegwell Road / Sandwich Road, Cliffsend, Ramsgate, Kent
opening_hours: Viewable from the green at any time.
accessibility: On a roadside grass area.
tips: Low winter sun from the south lights the hull side facing the road.
best_time: Late afternoon and blue hour.
facilities: Pegwell Bay Country Park car park and toilets are a short distance south.

name: Pegwell Bay Country Park bird hide
summary: A hide and level sea-wall path overlooking the saltmarsh and mudflats of the Stour estuary, part of a National Nature Reserve.
description: Pegwell Bay Country Park sits on reclaimed land beside the mouth of the River Stour and is the main public access point to the Sandwich and Pegwell Bay National Nature Reserve, run by Kent Wildlife Trust. A firm, wheelchair-friendly path runs round the sea wall, with a bird hide overlooking the saltmarsh and mudflats. In autumn and winter large numbers of waders and wildfowl feed here, including dunlin, sanderling and grey plover, and seals are seen in the estuary. In spring nightingales, cuckoos and warblers arrive in the scrub, and in summer the park's grassland is good for butterflies. The saltmarsh and mudflats themselves are closed to the public, so the hide and sea wall are the places to watch from. A café and toilets are on site.
address: Pegwell Bay Country Park, Sandwich Road, Ramsgate, Kent
price: Free entry. Car park (Kent County Council) £1.30 per day Mon-Fri, £2 weekends and bank holidays (as published by KWT).
dogs: Dogs banned all year from the mudflats, saltmarsh, Pegwell beach and upper chalk shore; fenced dog zone in the park.
accessibility: Solid, wheelchair-accessible sea-wall path plus mown grass paths; disabled parking and accessible toilet.
tips: Waders come closest on a rising tide as it pushes them off the mud; check the tide table and arrive about 2 hours before high water.
best_time: September to March for waders and wildfowl; April-May for spring migrants; summer for butterflies.
tide: Rising tide brings feeding waders closer to the hide; at low tide birds are distant on the mud.
wildlife: Autumn/winter: dunlin, sanderling, grey plover, wildfowl, seals. Spring: nightingale, cuckoo, warblers. Summer: butterflies.
facilities: Hide: one bird hide in the country park, overlooking the saltmarsh (open whenever the park is open, free). Car park with disabled and bicycle parking, toilets including accessible toilet, café (Salty Seal).

name: Stonelees seal viewpoint, Pegwell Bay
summary: Land-based seal watching over the Stour estuary, from the end of Stonelees just past the Country Park.
description: Kent Wildlife Trust points seal-watchers to the end of Stonelees, a small nature reserve of scrub just beyond Pegwell Bay Country Park, from where seals can be seen hauled out on the sandbanks and mud of the Stour estuary. OpenStreetMap marks the seal colony on the flats a short way to the east. Seals in the Stour are best looked for in autumn and winter, when they rest on the banks around low tide. They are distant, so this is telephoto and spotting-scope territory: a 500-800 mm lens, heat-haze-free cool mornings and a low, steady position give the best chance. Never approach across the mudflats; they are closed to the public and the mud is dangerous. For closer views, seal-watching boat trips run from Ramsgate and Sandwich.
address: Stonelees, off Sandwich Road, Cliffsend, Kent
price: Free (park in Pegwell Bay Country Park, paid).
dogs: Dogs not allowed on the mudflats and saltmarsh.
accessibility: Paths through scrub; not surfaced beyond the country park.
tips: Low tide exposes the haul-out banks. Cool, overcast mornings reduce heat shimmer over the mud.
best_time: Autumn and winter, around low tide, mornings.
tide: Low tide, when sandbanks are exposed; the mudflats are dangerous and closed to the public.
wildlife: Seals on the Stour estuary, best seen autumn and winter (both harbour and grey seals use the estuary; species split not confirmed from the fetched source).
facilities: Viewpoint only, no hide building. Facilities in Pegwell Bay Country Park.

name: Seal-watching boat trips from Ramsgate and Sandwich
summary: Small-boat trips out to the seals of Pegwell Bay and the Stour, the closest way to photograph them.
description: Several small operators run seal trips along the North East Kent coast, taking passengers from Ramsgate Royal Harbour or Sandwich Quay round to the sandbanks of Pegwell Bay and the Stour where seals haul out. The Thanet Coast Project lists Go2Sea Boat Excursions (Ramsgate Royal Harbour, seal, wind farm and coastal trips; 07931 744788), River Runner Seal Trips (Sandwich Quay or Ramsgate Harbour, with full wheelchair access; 07955 465729) and Sea Searcher (Ramsgate Royal Harbour, harbour sightseeing and seal tours from 1 April; 07837 562076, 8am-4pm). Boats approach slowly and stay at a distance under marine wildlife-watching codes, so a 100-400 mm zoom is ideal; fast shutter speeds cope with the rocking boat. Overcast days avoid harsh reflections off wet fur.
opening_hours: Seasonal; Sea Searcher from 1 April. Book direct with each operator.
price: Set by each operator; not confirmed.
accessibility: River Runner advertises full wheelchair access.
tips: Ask the skipper which tide state the trip runs on: seals are on the banks around low water. Keep a dry bag for your camera.
best_time: Trips run mainly spring to autumn; seals present year-round.
tide: Seals haul out on sandbanks around low tide.
wildlife: Seals in Pegwell Bay and the Stour estuary.
facilities: Booking required with the operator; harbour car parks and facilities in Ramsgate. Operators must follow the Marine Wildlife Watching code (Thanet Coastal Codes) and WiSe guidance.

name: Sandwich Bay Bird Observatory
summary: A recording and ringing station on the dunes south of Pegwell Bay, with field centre, reserves and a hide.
description: Sandwich Bay Bird Observatory Trust looks after and records the wildlife of the Sandwich Bay coast, a sweep of dunes, shingle, grazing marsh and scrub south of the Stour mouth. Its field centre on Guilford Road welcomes visitors daily and is the place to check recent sightings and ringing news: the Trust records birds, moths, butterflies, dragonflies and plants, and publishes sightings on its website. The Trust manages several small reserves around the estate, and OpenStreetMap shows a Trust-operated bird hide on the coast south of the field centre. In spring and autumn the bay is a major landfall for migrants, and in summer the shingle beach holds nesting oystercatchers and ringed plover, while rare dune plants such as lizard orchid grow nearby. Access to the Sandwich Bay estate is by a private toll road.
address: Guilford Road, Sandwich Bay, Sandwich, Kent
opening_hours: Field centre welcomes visitors daily (hours not published on the pages checked; ring ahead).
price: Toll road into Sandwich Bay £7 per car (per KWT). Observatory facility charges not confirmed.
dogs: On the Sandwich Bay beach: off lead from the car park to Prince's enclosure, on lead within it, not allowed in the restricted area (KWT).
accessibility: A mobility scooter is available for hire at the observatory; paths elsewhere are sandy and unsurfaced.
tips: Check the sightings page before you go; after easterly winds in spring and autumn the bushes can be full of migrants.
best_time: April-May and August-October for migration; June-July for orchids, butterflies and breeding shorebirds.
tide: The beach and shore are best on a rising tide for waders; dunes and reserves are tide-independent.
wildlife: Spring/autumn migrants; summer breeding oystercatcher and ringed plover on the shingle; lizard orchid and other dune plants; moths, butterflies and dragonflies recorded by the Trust.
facilities: Hide: Trust-operated bird hide on the coast (OSM node 5829166932; name and opening not confirmed). Field centre with tea-making kitchen, accommodation and hall hire; mobility scooter hire. Toll road £7 per car.

name: Stodmarsh NNR: Reedbed, Tower and Marsh hides (Stodmarsh car park end)
summary: Kent's great reedbed reserve near Canterbury: bitterns, marsh harriers and bearded tits from a string of free hides.
description: Stodmarsh National Nature Reserve lies in the Stour valley north-east of Canterbury, about 25 minutes' drive from Birchington. Its reedbeds, lagoons, wet meadows and alder carr form one of the most important wetlands in the South East, protected as a Ramsar site, Special Protection Area and Special Area of Conservation and named one of England's 35 'spotlight' reserves. More than 200 bird species have been recorded. Bittern is the flagship species, alongside marsh harrier, hen harrier in winter, bearded tit, and sedge and reed warblers in summer; otters, water voles, beavers and eight species of bat also live here, with 17 kinds of dragonfly and damselfly. From the Natural England car park in Stodmarsh village, a path leads onto the reserve past the Reedbed Hide, the raised Tower Hide and the Marsh Hide, with the Lampen Wall path running out across the reedbed. Entry is free and the reserve is open at any time.
address: Stodmarsh National Nature Reserve car park, Stodmarsh, near Canterbury, Kent
price: Free entry; Stodmarsh village car park (Natural England) small voluntary charge (as of 2022).
accessibility: OSM tags the reserve as wheelchair-accessible in part; Tower Hide is tagged not wheelchair-accessible. Paths can be muddy in winter.
tips: Bitterns are most often seen flying low over the reeds early and late in the day, and in cold winter spells when they feed at reed edges. Bring a long lens and patience.
best_time: Dawn and dusk; winter for bittern, hen harrier and harrier roosts; May-June for booming bittern, warblers; June-August for dragonflies.
wildlife: Bittern (all year), marsh harrier (all year), hen harrier (winter), bearded tit, sedge and reed warblers (Apr-Sep), otter, water vole, beaver, 8 bat species, 17 dragonfly/damselfly species, Kentish neb moth.
facilities: Hides at this end: Reedbed Hide (51.30690, 1.18596), Tower Hide (51.31123, 1.18681; raised, not wheelchair-accessible per OSM), Marsh Hide (51.31186, 1.19348), plus two unnamed hides mapped near the Lampen Wall. All free and open at any time. Natural England car park with small voluntary charge; no café on site (Red Lion pub in the village, not confirmed).

name: Stodmarsh NNR: Grove Ferry hides (David Feast's and Harrison's Drove)
summary: The northern entrance to Stodmarsh from the A28 near Upstreet: hides over open lagoons, handy from Thanet.
description: Grove Ferry, on the River Stour by the A28 at Upstreet, is the northern gateway to Stodmarsh National Nature Reserve and the closest end to Birchington. From the Kent County Council car park, paths run along the river and into the reserve to hides overlooking open water, flooded meadows and reedbed. David Feast's Hide and Harrison's Drove Hide look over the lagoons where wildfowl and waders gather, and there is a further hide mapped close to the car park. This end of the reserve is good for marsh harriers quartering the reeds, wintering ducks, passage waders in spring and autumn, and in winter the chance of hen harrier at dusk. The Grove Ferry Inn by the bridge offers food. As at the other end, the reserve is free and open at all times, and the walk through connects to the Stodmarsh village hides.
address: Grove Ferry Picnic Site, Grove Ferry Hill, Upstreet, near Canterbury, Kent
price: Free entry; Grove Ferry car park (Kent County Council) has an obligatory charge.
accessibility: Riverside and reserve paths are mostly level; hides' wheelchair access not confirmed.
tips: The lagoons in front of David Feast's Hide are best in the morning with the sun behind you to the south-east.
best_time: Winter for wildfowl and harrier roost; April-May and August-September for passage waders; early morning light.
wildlife: Marsh harrier, bittern, wintering wildfowl, passage waders, hen harrier in winter (reserve species per Wikipedia).
facilities: Hides at this end: David Feast's Hide (51.31867, 1.20290), Harrison's Drove Hide (51.31571, 1.20486), unnamed hide near the car park (51.32020, 1.20493). Free, open at all times. Paid KCC car park; Grove Ferry Inn (pub) next to the bridge.

name: Oare Marshes (Kent Wildlife Trust): East Flood and Sea Wall hides
summary: Grazing marsh and scrapes on the Swale near Faversham, famous for close views of waders from the road and two hides.
description: Oare Marshes is a Kent Wildlife Trust reserve of grazing marsh, freshwater scrapes and saltings on the Swale north of Faversham, about 45 minutes' drive from Birchington. It is part of The Swale's protected wetlands (Ramsar, SPA and SSSI). The reserve is known for how close the birds are: the East Flood beside the approach road often has waders and ducks within easy camera range, and many photographers work simply from the roadside. Year-round there are barn and little owls, little egret and ringed plover; in spring bearded tits; in summer terns, garganey, little ringed plover and turtle dove; and in autumn and winter, the best seasons, black-tailed godwits in big flocks, brent geese, grey plover, curlew sandpiper on passage, hen harrier, merlin and short-eared owl. Access is restricted to the footpath and nature trail to protect the birds.
address: Harty Ferry Road, Oare, Faversham, Kent
opening_hours: Open at all times. Volunteer work parties on Mondays and Wednesdays can be noisy.
dogs: On a lead all year; must stay on the public right of way and out of water, ditches and saltmarsh.
accessibility: Seasonally wheelchair accessible: level compacted roadstone path to the sea hide, RADAR gates, disabled-only car park about 300 m from the East Flood hide. Full circuit may be impassable when wet.
tips: Arrive at the East Flood about 1-2 hours before a high tide on the Swale: the rising water pushes waders off the estuary onto the scrapes.
best_time: Autumn and winter best; spring and summer for terns, garganey and turtle dove. Evening light from the west over the East Flood.
tide: High tide on the Swale pushes waders onto the East Flood scrapes.
wildlife: All year: barn owl, little owl, little egret, ringed plover, corn bunting. Spring: bearded tit. Summer: common and little tern, garganey, little ringed plover, turtle dove. Winter: brent goose, black-tailed godwit, grey plover, hen harrier, merlin, short-eared owl, red-breasted merganser, rock pipit; autumn passage greenshank and curlew sandpiper.
facilities: Hides: East Flood hide (wheelchair-accessible, 51.34176, 0.89005) and Sea Wall Hide on the corner of the marsh (51.34454, 0.89670; OSM tags it not wheelchair-accessible). Free, open at all times. Paid car park opposite the Watch House at the end of Harty Ferry Road, bicycle parking. Toilets not confirmed.

name: Elmley National Nature Reserve, Isle of Sheppey
summary: A privately run 3,300-acre marsh reserve on Sheppey with hides near Kingshill Farm; ticketed entry, open four days a week.
description: Elmley is a 3,300-acre National Nature Reserve on the Isle of Sheppey, a working farm and wilderness of grazing marsh, fleets and saltmarsh beside the Swale, about an hour's drive from Birchington. It is run privately from Kingshill Farm, which also offers accommodation and events, and the team runs a curlew recovery project. Visitors drive along the farm track to the yard at Kingshill, where OpenStreetMap shows a cluster of hides and screens close to the car park overlooking the marsh. The open, roadless landscape gives huge skies and a sense of space that suits wildlife and landscape photographers alike, and staying overnight gives access to dawn and dusk light. Entry is by ticket only, with limited numbers, so book ahead.
address: Kingshill Farm, Elmley, Isle of Sheppey, Kent
opening_hours: Open Wednesday, Thursday, Saturday and Sunday; closed Monday, Tuesday and Friday. Hours in the reserve's opening-times PDF (not confirmed here).
price: Ticketed entry per adult, limited numbers, advance booking recommended (price not confirmed).
tips: Book a ticket online before you travel; overnight guests get the best light.
best_time: Winter for wildfowl and raptors over the marsh; spring for breeding waders (species not confirmed from the reserve's pages).
tide: High tide on the Swale pushes waders onto the marsh (general estuary behaviour, not confirmed for Elmley).
wildlife: Wetland and farmland birds; curlew recovery project. Detailed species list not confirmed from the reserve's own pages.
facilities: Hides: six hides/screens mapped in OSM around Kingshill Farm (51.3746-51.3775, 0.7843-0.7854), names not confirmed. Ticket only; visits team on 07931 315271. Car park at Kingshill.

name: Capel Fleet Raptor Viewpoint, Isle of Sheppey
summary: A roadside raised viewpoint over the Capel Fleet marshes on Sheppey, used for watching winter birds of prey.
description: On the Harty Road across eastern Sheppey, OpenStreetMap shows a raised Raptor Viewpoint within the Capel Fleet nature reserve, looking out over a huge, open expanse of grazing marsh and the Capel Fleet channel. Its name says what it is for: scanning the marshes for hunting birds of prey, especially on winter afternoons when they quarter the fields before roosting. It is a fine place for big-sky landscapes too, with the marsh flat to the horizon in every direction. The Harty Road continues to the old Harty Ferry crossing opposite Oare and to the Swale National Nature Reserve at Shellness. The viewpoint is free, open access, and can be combined with Elmley on the same day.
address: Harty Ferry Road, Eastchurch, Isle of Sheppey, Kent
accessibility: Roadside; mound access not confirmed.
tips: Late winter afternoons up to dusk; park considerately, the road is narrow.
best_time: Winter afternoons to dusk.
wildlife: Winter birds of prey (species not confirmed from an official source).
facilities: Viewpoint (OSM leisure=bird_hide 'Raptor Viewpoint'); no facilities.

name: Monkton Nature Reserve (orchids, butterflies, bats)
summary: A 16-acre former chalk quarry near Minster with 10 orchid species, 25 butterflies and a bat cave: Thanet's macro hotspot.
description: Monkton Nature Reserve occupies a 16-acre abandoned chalk quarry on the southern side of Thanet, a short drive from Birchington. It is run as a charity by the Thanet Countryside Trust for conservation and education. The chalk grassland on the quarry floor and slopes holds more than 350 species of flowering plant, including ten kinds of orchid, and 25 butterfly species have been recorded, which makes it ideal for macro photography in late spring and summer. There is woodland over 40 years old, ponds full of pond life, exposed chalk cliffs, a bat cave and a field study centre with trails and activities for children. Visit in the morning before butterflies warm up, when they sit still on grass heads with dew.
address: Canterbury Road, Monkton, near Ramsgate, Kent
opening_hours: Tue, Thu, Sat and Sun 10:00-16:00 (last entry 15:00); Fridays in school holidays only; closed bank holidays.
price: Admission charged (prices not published on the home page); members free.
tips: Orchids peak from late May to July; a macro lens of 90-105 mm and a diffuser handle the bright chalk well. Stick to paths.
best_time: May-July for orchids; June-August for butterflies; early morning for still, dewy insects.
wildlife: 10 orchid species and 350+ flowering plants (spring-summer), 25 butterfly species (summer), woodland birds, pond life; bats (bat cave).
facilities: Reserve car park, field study centre; entry within opening hours only.

name: Minster and Sevenscore marshes
summary: Open grazing marshes between Minster and the Stour: big flat skies, dykes, mist and winter wildfowl.
description: South of Minster the land drops into a wide, flat stretch of drained marsh, the eastern end of the former Wantsum Channel, running down to the River Stour and Richborough. Sevenscore Farm and the Minster and Monkton marshes are crossed by drainage dykes and a handful of public footpaths, with almost no buildings. This is landscape country rather than a formal reserve: misty autumn dawns, sheep and cattle on the levels, dyke reflections and huge skies, plus darker horizons to the south for night shots than in the Thanet towns. In winter the fields can hold wildfowl, waders and hunting birds of prey. The marshes adjoin the industrial area around Richborough and the new HVDC converter station, so choose compositions that face away from them.
opening_hours: Public footpaths only; the farmland is private.
dogs: Keep dogs on leads around livestock.
accessibility: Unsurfaced field paths, muddy in winter.
tips: Use OS maps to stay on rights of way; the marsh is flat, so stand on a bridge or bank for a little height.
best_time: Calm autumn and winter dawns for mist; winter afternoons for wildfowl and raptors.
wildlife: Wintering wildfowl, waders and birds of prey on the levels (not confirmed from an official source).

name: Quex Park gardens and Waterloo Tower
summary: Birchington's estate gardens: woodland walk, walled kitchen garden and a Regency bell tower for flowers and architecture.
description: Quex Park, on the southern edge of Birchington, combines the Powell-Cotton Museum, the Regency mansion of Quex House and its gardens. The gardens have lawns, a woodland walk and a historic walled kitchen garden, which offer flowers, fruit trees and old brick walls for close-up and macro work through the season. In the park stands the Waterloo Tower, a tall Grade II listed tower that is a striking architectural subject from the surrounding fields, especially against a dramatic sky. The garden is included with the museum day ticket. Quex Barn farm shop and restaurant sit beside the estate entrance.
address: Quex Park, Park Lane, Birchington, Kent
opening_hours: Museum and gardens 2026 season 14 Feb - 1 Nov: term time Fri-Sun and bank holidays 11:00-16:00; school holidays Wed-Sun 11:00-16:00. Check website.
price: Museum day ticket includes gardens: adult £9, concession £8, child 4-16 £7 (2026, per local press).
accessibility: AccessAble guide published for the museum.
tips: The Waterloo Tower can be photographed from public paths around the park when the museum is closed.
best_time: Spring and summer for flowers; autumn for woodland colour.
facilities: Parking at Quex Park; Quex Barn restaurant and farm shop.

name: Northdown Park, Cliftonville
summary: A large council park with mature trees and lawns near Foreness, good for autumn colour and garden birds.
description: Northdown Park is a large public park run by Thanet District Council in Cliftonville, between Margate and Broadstairs and a short walk inland from Foreness Point and Botany Bay. It has wide lawns, mature trees and shrubberies around the historic Northdown House, plus a playground and café. For photographers it is a sheltered alternative when the coast is too windy: autumn leaf colour, frosty winter mornings, flowers in spring and summer, and garden birds that are used to people. Because it is close to the coast, the trees can also hold migrant birds after easterly winds in spring and autumn.
accessibility: Mostly level paths and lawns.
tips: Combine a morning at Foreness Point with the park's trees on a migration day.
best_time: October-November for autumn colour; spring and autumn for migrants.
wildlife: Garden and woodland birds; occasional migrants (not confirmed from an official source).
facilities: Playground; parking nearby.

name: Margate Main Sands sunset
summary: Margate's big sandy beach faces west-north-west: the summer sun sets over the sea and the wet sand glows.
description: Margate's Main Sands curve from the harbour arm westwards towards Westbrook, a broad sandy beach backed by the seafront, the clock tower and Dreamland. Because the bay faces north-west, it is one of the best places in Thanet to watch the sun set over the sea in late spring and summer, and its famous skies are the reason J.M.W. Turner came here so often. At low tide the sand stretches far out and holds pools and wet reflections; silhouettes of walkers, dogs and swimmers against the low sun make lively compositions. After sunset, turn east for blue-hour views of the harbour arm, the Turner Contemporary and the lit seafront.
dogs: Seasonal beach dog restrictions in summer; check signage.
accessibility: Level promenade with ramps to the sand.
tips: From May to August the sun sets roughly over the sea; in winter it sets behind Westbrook and the land.
best_time: Summer sunsets; blue hour afterwards towards the harbour.
tide: Low tide gives wide reflective sand; high tide reaches the sea wall.
facilities: Seafront cafés, toilets and pay car parks; Margate station opposite the beach.

name: Stone Bay, Broadstairs
summary: A quiet chalk bay north of Viking Bay with a sea wall walk, beach huts and a wide reef for pools.
description: Stone Bay lies just north of Viking Bay in Broadstairs, reached by steps from the clifftop or along the promenade from the main beach. It is quieter than Viking Bay, with chalk cliffs, a long line of beach huts and a broad chalk reef exposed at low tide. The Thanet Coast Project made one of its seashore safari films here, so it is a proven rock-pooling spot for macro work. Facing east, it catches the sunrise straight out over the sea, and the beach huts and promenade make strong leading lines in low morning light.
dogs: Seasonal dog rules in summer; check signage.
accessibility: Steps from the clifftop; promenade from Viking Bay is level.
tips: Walk on from Viking Bay at sunrise; low tide for the reef.
best_time: Sunrise (east-facing); low spring tides for pools.
tide: Low tide exposes the reef; the rising tide reaches the sea wall and cuts off the walk round the points.
wildlife: Shore life on the reef.
facilities: Facilities in Broadstairs town.

name: Thanet north coast: noctilucent clouds and northern horizon
summary: Birchington's north-facing seafront gives an unobstructed sea horizon for summer night-shining clouds and aurora alerts.
description: Most of Thanet's north coast, from Minnis Bay through Birchington, Westgate and Margate, looks out over the Thames Estuary with nothing but sea to the north. That empty northern horizon is valuable for two night-sky subjects that hug the north: noctilucent clouds, the electric-blue 'night-shining' clouds that appear low in the north to north-west after sunset in June and July, and the aurora, which in strong geomagnetic storms can be visible or photographable from southern England as a glow low in the north. Minnis Bay is the darkest easy access point, with the Wantsum marsh behind it; Margate's seafront is brighter but has the harbour arm as foreground. Watch aurora alerts and simply turn up with a tripod.
accessibility: Level promenade.
tips: For noctilucent clouds, look north-west 60-90 minutes after sunset in mid-June to mid-July; for aurora, a camera often records colour your eye cannot see.
best_time: Late May to early August for noctilucent clouds; any clear, dark night during strong geomagnetic activity for aurora.
tide: Not important; keep to the promenade in the dark.
facilities: Car park and toilets at Minnis Bay.

name: Westbrook Undercliffe Nature Park, Margate
summary: A green strip beneath the cliffs between Westgate and Margate, handy for coastal flowers and insects.
description: Between Westgate and Margate's Main Sands, the promenade at Westbrook runs below the chalk cliffs past a small undercliff green space mapped as Westbrook Undercliffe Nature Park. It offers coastal plants and insects close to the promenade, a sheltered spot for macro on breezy days, and easy access to the Westbrook beach and its chalk foreshore. It sits on the walking route along the coast from Birchington to Margate, so it is easy to include on a coastal photo walk heading east towards the Main Sands for sunset.
accessibility: Level promenade alongside.
tips: Combine with a sunset at Margate Main Sands a short walk east.
best_time: Late spring and summer for flowers and insects.
tide: Low tide exposes the Westbrook foreshore.
wildlife: Coastal plants and insects (species not confirmed).
